title: Compound nouns 2: verb + preposition
subtitle: a takeover, a breakdown, the outcome
summary: Use nouns made from phrasal verbs - takeover, crackdown, breakdown, outcome - to talk about news, business and everyday life.

lesson.heading: Nouns made from phrasal verbs
lesson.text: Many English nouns are simply a phrasal verb written as one word or with a hyphen. From *to take over* we get a **takeover**, and from *to work out* we get a **workout**. The plural is regular: just add *s*.

examples.text: The **takeover** was announced on Monday.
examples.note: = one company taking control of another

examples.text: She does three **workouts** a week at the gym.

lesson.note: These nouns usually feel informal, which is why journalists like them so much.

lesson.heading: Journalism
lesson.text: Newspaper reports are full of these compounds because they are short and dramatic. A **walkout** is a strike, a **crackdown** is firm action to stop something, and a **break-up** is a collapse.

examples.text: In response to the pay offer, there was a **walkout** at the factory.
There is going to be a **crackdown** on public spending.
examples.note: = action to stop or reduce it

examples.text: An inquiry into the recent **breakout** from the local prison has recommended tighter security.
Last month saw a tremendous **shake-up** in personnel.
Last week we reported on the **break-up** of the mayor's marriage.

lesson.heading: The economy
lesson.text: Business English uses another family of these nouns. Note that **turnover** means the money passing through a company, while **cutbacks** are reductions in what a company spends.

examples.text: The **takeover** of one of our leading hotel chains has just been announced.
We're trying to find some new **outlets** for our products.
Take your things to the **check-out** to pay for them.
**Cutbacks** will be essential until the recession is over.
Our profit was 1,000 pounds on a **turnover** of 10,000 pounds.
The banks were given a huge **bailout** by the government.
examples.note: = money given to save a company from failure

lesson.heading: Aspects of modern life
rows: paper with computer information printed on it
lesson.note: What the computer produces depends on the **input**. A **breakthrough** has been made in AIDS research.

lesson.heading: General use
lesson.text: These compounds work in everyday situations too. The **outlook** is what we expect to happen, the **outcome** is how something ends, and **drawbacks** are the negative aspects of a plan.

examples.text: Many of the problems were caused by a **breakdown** in communications.
The **outlook** for tomorrow is good - sunny in most places.
There are **drawbacks** as well as advantages to every situation.
The **outcome** of the meeting was not very satisfactory.
TV companies always welcome **feedback** from viewers.

lesson.heading: More general compounds
lesson.text: A few more worth learning: the **outset** is the start, a **set-up** is a situation or the way something is organised, and an **outbreak** is the start of something unpleasant.

examples.text: It was clear from the **outset** that the **set-up** would cause problems.
We parked in a **lay-by** on the **bypass**.
examples.note: a lay-by = a parking space beside a road; a bypass = a road avoiding a town centre

examples.text: The **outbreak** of war took many people by surprise.

lesson.text: Same parts, different order, different meaning: **outlook** is a prospect but a **look-out** is a person watching for danger; an **outlay** is money spent but a **layout** is the way something is arranged.

exercises.prompt: Match each compound noun with its synonym.
Match these compound nouns with their synonyms.
The explosion at the reactor produced radioactive ___ that drifted over three countries.
exercises.explanation: Fallout is the radioactive dust that falls out of the atmosphere after a nuclear explosion.

exercises.prompt: After months of overwork he had a nervous ___ and was off work for a year.
exercises.explanation: A breakdown is a failure - of a machine, of communications or of a person's health.

exercises.prompt: I can easily get you a computer ___ of the latest figures.
exercises.explanation: A printout is paper on which computer information has been printed.

exercises.prompt: Complete the headline: 'Police plan ___ on vandalism'.
exercises.explanation: A crackdown is firm action taken to stop or reduce something.

exercises.prompt: Complete the headline: 'Prime Minister announces cabinet ___'.
exercises.explanation: A shake-up is a big change in the way something is organised.

exercises.prompt: Complete the headline: 'Football star injured in pre-game ___'.
exercises.explanation: A workout is an exercise session, from to work out.
An outbreak is the sudden start of something unpleasant, such as a disease or a war. A breakout is an escape from prison.

exercises.prompt: Which compound nouns belong to the world of business, and which describe the start or end of something?
Put the words in order to make a sentence about a traffic delay.
exercises.answer: Because of the accident there was a three-mile tailback
exercises.explanation: A tailback is a long queue of traffic - it tails back from the vehicle at the head of the queue.

exercises.statement: Police are warning of an increased number of break-ins in this area - that is, of burglaries.
exercises.explanation: Correct. A break-in is a burglary: burglars break in to buildings.

exercises.statement: If our plans have suffered a setback, it means they have suddenly become much easier.
exercises.explanation: A setback is an obstacle in the way of progress - something has set us back.

exercises.statement: There was a surprisingly large turnout at the concert means a lot of people came.
exercises.explanation: Correct. A turnout is the audience or crowd - people turn out to attend something.

exercises.prompt: I love having a ___ on Sundays - I don't get up until eleven.
exercises.explanation: To lie in is to stay in bed longer than usual, so a lie-in is a long morning in bed.
